stem: Which organism causes cholera?

options.content: *Vibrio cholerae*
options.rationale: Correct: a comma-shaped, flagellated bacterium.

options.content: *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*
options.rationale: This bacterium causes tuberculosis.

options.content: *Plasmodium falciparum*
options.rationale: This protoctist causes malaria.

options.content: *Mycobacterium bovis*
options.rationale: This bacterium causes TB in cattle and can infect humans.

explanation: Cholera is caused by the bacterium *Vibrio cholerae*.

stem: How is cholera transmitted?

options.content: By swallowing water or food contaminated with infected faeces
options.rationale: Correct: the faecal-oral route.

options.content: By breathing in droplets released when an infected person coughs nearby
options.rationale: This is how TB spreads, not cholera.

options.content: By the bite of an infected female mosquito feeding at night
options.rationale: This is how malaria spreads.

options.content: By sexual contact or by sharing needles with an infected person
options.rationale: These routes transmit HIV.

explanation: *V. cholerae* is passed in faeces and swallowed in contaminated water or food: the **faecal-oral route**.

stem: Cholera toxin causes intestinal epithelial cells to secrete chloride ions into the lumen of the small intestine. Why does this cause watery diarrhoea?

options.content: The water potential of the lumen falls, so water leaves the cells and blood by osmosis
options.rationale: Correct: solutes lower the water potential of the lumen and water follows.

options.content: Chloride ions digest the epithelium, so blood plasma leaks out through the damaged lining
options.rationale: The lining is not digested; water moves by osmosis.

options.content: The water potential of the lumen rises, so water moves out of the lumen into the blood
options.rationale: Adding ions lowers the water potential of the lumen; water moves into the lumen.

options.content: Chloride ions block the active transport of water into the blood
options.rationale: Water is not actively transported; it moves by osmosis.

explanation: Chloride ions (followed by sodium ions) in the lumen **lower its water potential**, so water moves out of the epithelial cells and blood into the lumen by **osmosis**.
hints: What happens to water potential when solutes are added?

stem: Why does an oral rehydration solution contain glucose as well as sodium salts?

options.content: Glucose kills *Vibrio cholerae* in the small intestine before it can multiply further
options.rationale: Glucose is not an antibiotic.

options.content: Glucose and sodium ions are co-transported into cells, and water follows
options.rationale: Correct: the sodium-glucose co-transporter is not affected by the toxin.

options.content: Glucose provides respiratory energy to replace the energy lost in the diarrhoea
options.rationale: Some energy is supplied, but its main role is to drive sodium and water uptake.

options.content: Glucose raises the water potential of the lumen so water is pushed out
options.rationale: Glucose lowers water potential; its role is to be absorbed with sodium.

explanation: Sodium-glucose **co-transporter** proteins still work. Absorbing glucose and sodium lowers the water potential of the epithelial cells, so water is absorbed by osmosis.
hints: Which membrane protein carries glucose and sodium ions together?

stem: How is *Mycobacterium bovis* most commonly passed to humans?

options.content: In water contaminated with faeces from infected cattle
options.rationale: This is the route for cholera, not bovine TB.

options.content: By ticks that feed on cattle and then on humans
options.rationale: TB is not spread by ticks.

options.content: Through cuts on the hands when handling cattle feed
options.rationale: TB is not usually spread through skin cuts.

options.content: In unpasteurised milk from infected cattle
options.rationale: Correct: pasteurisation kills the bacteria.

explanation: *M. bovis* reaches humans mainly in **unpasteurised milk**; pasteurising milk and testing cattle prevent this.

stem: Why are people living with HIV much more likely to develop active tuberculosis?

options.content: HIV and the TB bacterium are carried in the same droplets so they always infect together
options.rationale: They are different pathogens with different routes; co-infection is not automatic.

options.content: HIV destroys T-helper cells, so latent TB bacteria are no longer kept in check
options.rationale: Correct: weakened cell-mediated immunity lets latent infection become active.

options.content: HIV converts into TB bacteria inside the lungs
options.rationale: A virus cannot turn into a bacterium.

options.content: Antiretroviral drugs damage the lungs and allow bacteria to enter
options.rationale: Antiretroviral therapy reduces TB risk by restoring immunity.

explanation: Latent TB is held in check by the immune system. HIV destroys **T-helper cells**, so the bacteria can multiply and active TB develops.

stem: Why is the treatment for tuberculosis at least six months long and given as a combination of several antibiotics?

options.content: The bacteria are viruses that hide inside cells, so ordinary antibiotics act very slowly
options.rationale: TB is caused by bacteria, not viruses.

options.content: The BCG vaccine must be given at the same time and takes six months to work
options.rationale: BCG is a vaccine given to babies, not part of the treatment course.

options.content: The bacteria grow slowly, some hide in macrophages, and drug combinations limit resistance
options.rationale: Correct: slow growth, hidden bacteria and the risk of selecting resistant mutants.

options.content: Each antibiotic kills the bacteria in a different organ of the body, so all of them are needed
options.rationale: The drugs are combined to prevent resistance, not because each works in one organ.

explanation: *M. tuberculosis* divides slowly and can survive inside macrophages and in damaged tissue, so a long course is needed. A bacterium is very unlikely to carry mutations resisting **several** drugs at once, so combinations reduce resistance.
hints: Think about how fast the bacteria grow and where they hide.

stem: What is the main purpose of DOTS in tuberculosis control?

options.content: To vaccinate all contacts of a patient against tuberculosis with BCG
options.rationale: DOTS is about treatment, not vaccination.

options.content: To test milk for *Mycobacterium bovis*
options.rationale: Milk is made safe by pasteurisation; DOTS is a treatment programme.

options.content: To isolate patients in hospital for six months so they cannot infect others
options.rationale: Most DOTS patients are treated in the community.

options.content: To make sure patients take every dose and complete the full course
options.rationale: Correct: directly observed treatment improves completion.

explanation: In **DOTS** a health worker or trained supporter watches each dose being taken, so the course is completed and drug resistance is less likely.

stem: A person with latent tuberculosis infection has no symptoms and does not pass the bacteria on.
explanation: True. In latent TB the bacteria are walled off and inactive; only active lung TB is infectious.

stem: Antibiotics are the most important treatment for saving the lives of people with severe cholera.
explanation: False. Death is caused by dehydration, so **rehydration** (oral or intravenous) saves lives; antibiotics only shorten the illness.

stem: Match each control measure with the way it reduces disease.

right.content: Gives immunity against severe childhood TB
Reduces airborne droplet transmission of TB
Kills *Vibrio cholerae* before water is drunk

explanation: Each measure breaks a different transmission route or builds immunity.

stem: Choose the correct words.

payload.template: Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium {{blank:a}} and is spread mainly by {{blank:b}}. Babies are protected by the {{blank:c}} vaccine. Bacteria resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin cause {{blank:d}}.

explanation: *M. tuberculosis*, droplets, BCG, and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB).

stem: Name the type of cell in the lungs that engulfs *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* but in which the bacteria can survive.
explanation: TB bacteria are engulfed by **macrophages** in the alveoli but resist digestion and survive inside them.

stem: In a hypothetical cholera outbreak in a rural district, 640 cases and 22 deaths were recorded. Calculate the case fatality rate as a percentage. Give your answer to two decimal places.
explanation: Case fatality rate $= \dfrac{22}{640} \times 100 = 3.44\%$. Dividing cases by deaths (640 ÷ 22) inverts the fraction.
workedSolution: 1. Case fatality rate $= \dfrac{22}{640} \times 100 = 3.44\%$. Dividing cases by deaths (640 ÷ 22) inverts the fraction.

stem:
A hypothetical district recorded the number of new active TB cases each year before and after antiretroviral therapy became widely available.

| Year | New active TB cases |
|---|---|
| Before wide antiretroviral therapy | 1480 |
| Five years later | 1110 |

Calculate the percentage decrease in new active TB cases.
explanation:
1. Decrease $= 1480 - 1110 = 370$.
2. Percentage decrease $= \dfrac{370}{1480} \times 100 = 25\%$.
3. Dividing by the later value (1110) gives 33.3%, which is wrong: always divide by the starting value.
4. A plausible explanation: therapy restores T-helper cells, so fewer latent infections become active.
workedSolution:
1. Decrease $= 1480 - 1110 = 370$.
2. Percentage decrease $= \dfrac{370}{1480} \times 100 = 25\%$.
3. Dividing by the later value (1110) gives 33.3%, which is wrong: always divide by the starting value.
4. A plausible explanation: therapy restores T-helper cells, so fewer latent infections become active.
hints: Divide the decrease by the original number.

stem: Explain how *Vibrio cholerae* causes severe dehydration.

points.description: Bacteria attach to (epithelial cells of) the small intestine and release a toxin
The toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted (through channels) into the lumen
This lowers the water potential of the lumen (sodium ions follow)
Water moves from cells / blood into the lumen by osmosis and is lost as watery diarrhoea

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The bacteria that survive the stomach attach to the epithelium of the small intestine and release cholera toxin. The toxin enters the epithelial cells and makes them secrete chloride ions into the lumen, followed by sodium ions. This lowers the water potential of the lumen, so water moves out of the cells and blood by osmosis and is lost in large volumes of watery diarrhoea, causing dehydration.

explanation: Bacteria → toxin → chloride ions out → water potential of lumen falls → osmosis → diarrhoea.
hints: Follow the chloride ions, then the water.

stem: Suggest why the 2008-09 cholera outbreak in Zimbabwe spread so widely, with reference to biological, social and economic factors.

points.description: Biological: carriers / people with mild symptoms spread bacteria without knowing; bacteria survive in water
Water treatment and piped supplies failed, so people used unsafe sources
Sewage systems broke down / burst sewers contaminated water sources
Health services were under strain / lack of funds for chemicals, repairs or staff delayed treatment and reporting; or movement of people spread it to new areas

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Infected people without symptoms continued to pass bacteria in their faeces. In towns, water treatment and piped supplies had failed and sewers had burst, so faeces contaminated the water that people collected from wells and streams. There was little money for water-treatment chemicals and repairs, and clinics were short of staff, so cases were treated and reported late. People travelling to rural homes carried the infection to new areas.

explanation: Credit specific, accurate factors linked to transmission; avoid blaming individuals.
hints: Think about water, sewage, health services and carriers.

stem: Explain why stopping a course of TB treatment early can lead to multidrug-resistant TB.

points.description: Some bacteria survive when treatment stops early (they are not all killed)
Survivors are more likely to be those with (chance) mutations giving resistance; resistance arises by mutation, not caused by the drug
They multiply and are passed on, so the resistant form becomes more common (natural selection)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: If treatment stops before all bacteria are killed, the survivors are most likely to be bacteria that happen to carry mutations making them less sensitive to the drugs. These multiply and can be passed to other people, so resistant strains become more common by natural selection.

explanation: Resistance comes from random mutation; the antibiotic only selects.
hints: Do antibiotics cause mutations, or select them?

stem:
In a hypothetical cholera treatment centre, adults with moderate dehydration were given either oral rehydration salts (ORS) by mouth or plain water by mouth after a first litre of intravenous fluid. The volume of intravenous fluid each patient needed afterwards was recorded.

| Patient | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ORS group / dm³ | 3 | 5 | 4 | 6 | 4 | 5 | 3 | 4 |
| Plain water group / dm³ | 7 | 6 | 8 | 7 | 9 | 6 | 8 | 7 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean volume of intravenous fluid needed by the ORS group, in dm³, to two decimal places.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean for the plain water group, in dm³, to two decimal places.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the ORS group needed less intravenous fluid.

points.description: ORS contains glucose and sodium ions, which are absorbed together by co-transporter proteins (not affected by the toxin)
This lowers the water potential of the epithelial cells / blood
So water is absorbed from the intestine by osmosis, replacing water lost; plain water alone is not absorbed as well

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: ORS supplies glucose and sodium ions, which are absorbed together through sodium-glucose co-transporter proteins that the toxin does not affect. Their uptake lowers the water potential of the epithelial cells and blood, so water follows by osmosis. Plain water without solutes is not absorbed as effectively while chloride is being secreted, so more fluid had to be given into a vein.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest two reasons why the results should be treated with caution.

points.description: Small sample (only 8 per group), so results may be due to chance
Patients may differ in severity of dehydration / body mass, or the groups were not randomised or blinded

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Only eight patients were in each group, so chance differences matter, and their initial dehydration and body mass may have differed between the groups.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: True or false: these data show that ORS kills *Vibrio cholerae* in the intestine.
parts.explanation: False. ORS replaces water and ions; it has no effect on the bacteria.

explanation: ORS works through sodium-glucose co-transport, so less intravenous fluid is needed.
hints: Which membrane protein still works during cholera?

stem: Sipho, a miner from Gweru, has had a cough for five weeks, night sweats and weight loss. A sputum test confirms active pulmonary tuberculosis. He shares a small room with four other workers. An HIV test is offered to him as part of routine care.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the bacterium most likely to have caused Sipho's TB.
parts.explanation: Pulmonary TB passed between people is caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why Sipho's roommates are at high risk of infection.

points.description: TB is spread by airborne droplets when he coughs / talks
Crowded, (poorly ventilated) room means close, prolonged contact / high concentration of droplets

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Sipho releases bacteria in droplets when he coughs. In a small, crowded room his roommates breathe in these droplets for long periods.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest why an HIV test is part of routine TB care.

points.description: HIV weakens the immune system / destroys T-helper cells, making active TB more likely
If positive, antiretroviral therapy can start, improving the outcome of TB treatment / reducing risk of death

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: HIV greatly raises the risk of latent TB becoming active, so many TB patients also have HIV. Knowing his status means antiretroviral therapy can be started alongside TB treatment, improving his chances of recovery.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which measure best protects the roommates?

options.content: Giving all of them a single dose of penicillin
options.rationale: A single dose would not treat TB and penicillin is not used for TB.

options.content: Giving all of them BCG regardless of age
options.rationale: BCG protects adults poorly; it is given to babies.

options.content: Tracing and testing them, and treating any active TB found
options.rationale: Correct: contact tracing finds and treats cases early.

options.content: Asking them to drink only pasteurised milk
options.rationale: This prevents *M. bovis* infection, not droplet spread from Sipho.

parts.explanation: Contact tracing and testing finds infected contacts early.

explanation: Droplet spread, crowding, HIV co-infection and contact tracing.
hints: Think about the route of transmission and the immune system.
